title: Quantinuum Aligns Software Development For Quantum Hardware Generations
author: Jeff Burt

Quantinuum Aligns Software Development For Quantum Hardware Generations

Jeff Burt

Jeff
Burt

Published
tue 17 Nov 2026 // 15:39 UTC

A week rarely goes by without news of significant advancements in the ongoing development of quantum computing, whether it is around error correction and fault tolerance, architectures and infrastructure, post-quantum cryptography, or tighter integrations between quantum and classical HPC systems.None of this is lost on enterprises, which are increasingly investigating how they can use the technology now and really benefit from it when more practical, scalable, and fault-tolerant systems begin to emerge in force in the coming years. According to analysts with global consultancy McKinsey & Co, more than 300 organizations across the global are working with quantum computing providers, and even more are experimenting with the technology.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

“Many business leaders now accept that quantum technology is coming sooner than they first expected, and they’re taking steps today to capture a competitive advantage,” they wrote in a report last month. “Faced with quantum technology’s rapid pace of development and the scale of its implications, leaders are now forced to reconsider their action plans. ... Quantum technology companies are hitting milestones more quickly than they initially predicted, and many have ambitious road maps that put the expected arrival of fault-tolerant quantum computing within the next few years.”Included in the ambitious roadmaps for many such vendors is the development of full-stack quantum offerings, moving beyond creating qubits and the hardware that goes around them to including software, developer tools, capabilities for hybrid quantum-classical and cloud environments, AI integrations, and APIs for optimization.It was a driving force behind Intel’s bid to buy quantum software maker Classiq for $2.3 billion. In announcing the deal late last month, Intel chief technology officer Pushkar Ranade explained that Intel had spent a decade building its quantum chips and SDK and running its quantum operation as something akin to a science project. Having Classiq in the fold “moves our quantum computing group from just a research-and-development focus to an actual quantum computing business,” Ranade said.The list of quantum companies building out full-stack capabilities includes IBM, D-Wave, Rigetti, and IonQ, among others. Quantinuum is another one, with the vendor matching its generations of quantum systems and as-a-service offerings (below) with advances in software – such as its InQuanto and Quantum Origin applications – and developer tools, from its Nexus developer platform two years ago to the toolkit for Guppy, its Python-based programming language.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

The growing attention by vendors on quantum software and developer tools “tells us the field is becoming more focused on what it takes to make quantum computing useful,” Josh Savory, senior director of offering management for Quantinuum, tells The Next Platform. “Qubit count matters, but customers ultimately need accurate answers at the speed their applications require. That takes highly accurate hardware, scalable error correction, software, and integration with classical computing. Customers should start preparing now. Building application expertise, testing error-corrected programs, and integrating quantum computation into classical workflows all take time.”The five-year-old company closely co-designs the hardware, error correction, and compilers with the developer tools, which Savory says lets developers take advantage of advances in the underlying hardware as quickly as possible.To that end, Quantinuum – which was formed in 2021 in the merger of Honeywell’s quantum division and quantum software company Cambridge Quantum Computing – earlier this month unveiled a new roadmap for its Nexus platform (below), outlining new capabilities with the upcoming next-generation hardware leading up to Apollo, the vendor’s first fault-tolerant system scheduled for 2029.

The company last year launched Helios (below), it’s third-generation trapped-ion quantum system that includes 98 qubits and which in October reached 99.9995 percent accuracy – five errors in a million operations – which company executives said was within the target range for Apollo. Along with Helios, Quantinuum includes such capabilities in Nexus as customized error suppression to optimize code performance, prebuilt primitives and logical qubits with proprietary codes, and the InQuanto quantum chemistry platform.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

More Nexus advancements are scheduled for next year, when the vendor runs out its Sol system, and then again with Apollo two years after that.

Savoy points to Guppy FT – a fault-tolerant programming framework and extension of the Guppy language – as an example of how Quantinuum connects software development with the company’s architecture, allowing developers to focus on algorithms while specialists improve how the algorithms are protected and executed. The vendor released Guppy FT and Guppy Algorithms – an open-source library of reusable building blocks and algorithmic primitives – in September.“The Nexus roadmap extends that connection across hardware generations,” he says. “We want the applications, workflows, and expertise customers build today to become more valuable as the systems advance. Our full stack strategy also focuses on integrating our tools across the broader ecosystem. Nexus supports tools developers already use, including [Nvidia’s] CUDA-Q and Q# [open source language created by Microsoft], and is designed to fit into cloud, on-premises, and in high-performance computing environments. The aim is to give developers an integrated path while supporting the broader ecosystem.”Pacing the development of the software and development tools with the hardware advancements will be important as more organizations begin growing their use of quantum computing. Savoy says that 215 companies are building on Nexus, with job submissions increasing 10x in the 12 months through August when compared with the previous 12 months.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

The release of the Nexus roadmap comes amid a number of other efforts by Quantinuum. Along with the error-corrections results from Helios in October, the vendor earlier this month announced it had upgraded the Reimei quantum computer housed at the RIKEN institute in Japan from its 20-qubit H1 system to a 56-qubit H2 computer.The H2 system will allow RIKEN scientists to combine quantum computing, supercomputing, and AI. In a separate announcement, Quantinuum, RIKEN, and Japanese multinational conglomerate SoftBank also explore how quantum systems can be directly connected to AI datacenters in Japan.Quantinuum in the third quarter also reported $9.1 million in revenue, a 233 percent year-over-year increase from $2.7 million and pushed its full-year revenue outlook from $31 million to $34 million. Savoy says its co-development efforts will help.“The important distinction is between developing supported error-corrected applications today and delivering universal fault tolerance at scale,” he says. “We are enabling the former while working toward the latter. Our hardware, software, and commercial ecosystem are parts of one strategy: give customers a reason to build with Quantinuum today and a path to carry that investment into the fault-tolerant era.”
